extracted.intended_audience: prospective and practicing K–8 / middle-school mathematics teachers and college faculty who teach them
extracted.subtask_short: discrete math course for middle-school teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and curricular recommendations for designing and teaching activity-based discrete mathematics courses (undergraduate or graduate level) aimed at preparing prospective and practicing middle-school/K–8 teachers. Covers content priorities, pedagogical approaches, sample activities, course formats, and assessment suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: NCTM recommended content areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Three important areas of discrete mathematics—combinatorics, iteration and recursion, and vertex-edge graphs—"should be an integral part of the school mathematics curriculum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat combinatorics (systematic counting), iteration and recursion (modeling sequential step-by-step change), and vertex-edge graphs (modeling paths, networks, relationships) as core topics to be spanned across K–12 grade levels. Use Navigation series recommendations to guide grade-by-grade sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent situations with vertex-edge graphs and adjacency matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: "Represent concrete and abstract situations by using vertex-edge graphs and represent vertex-edge graphs with adjacency matrices."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to model real-world and abstract problems as graphs and to translate graphs into adjacency matrices as a representation tool; include concrete classroom modeling activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe and apply graph properties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Describe and apply properties of graphs, such as vertex degrees, edge weights, directed edges, and isomorphism (whether two graphs are the 'same')."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks that require identification and use of degree, edge weights, directedness, and graph isomorphism; provide activities that surface these properties and require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graphs to solve path/network problems (Euler, Hamilton, MST, shortest paths)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Use graphs to solve problems related to paths, circuits, and networks in real-world and abstract settings, including explicit use of Euler paths, Hamilton paths, minimum spanning trees, and shortest paths."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include classical path/circuit/network problems and real-world modeling; emphasize problem-solving strategies and algorithmic approaches relevant to each topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and apply vertex coloring
rubrics_metrics.description: "Understand and apply vertex coloring to solve problems related to avoiding conflicts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use map-coloring and scheduling conflicts as motivating examples; include kinesthetic/human-graph coloring activities so students experience conflict-avoidance problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algorithmic thinking with graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: "Use algorithmic thinking to solve problems related to vertex-edge graphs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach stepwise procedures, tree-search strategies, and simple algorithms (e.g., greedy MST heuristic, shortest-path intuition) and have students practice formalizing and reasoning about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graphs to solve optimization problems
rubrics_metrics.description: "Use vertex-edge graphs to solve optimization problems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include optimization formulations (e.g., minimize routes, colorings, matchings) and problem-solving tasks that require students to compare solutions and justify optimality or heuristic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity-based pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials and courses are "activities-based" and designed to help teachers develop mathematical thinking and reasoning skills using an activities-based approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center instruction on carefully sequenced hands-on activities that model the pedagogical style teachers should emulate; minimize lecture and maximize guided inquiry, group work, and whole-class discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read–investigate–reflect learning cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should "read a bit, then figure things out a bit, then read some more, reflect, and figure things out some more" so they imitate mathematical behavior and develop habits of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure class sessions and assignments to alternate short readings with exploration and reflection; use the cycle to move students from imitation to independent mathematical thinking over a semester.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop problem-solving skills and habits of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The course focuses on "developing problem-solving skills and habits of mind that engage and invite the prospective K–8 teacher to think mathematically."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize activities that ask Why? How do you know? What happens if we change the problem slightly? so students learn conjecturing, experimentation, justification, and perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully sequenced activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The curriculum provides a textbook, activity book, and classroom guide with "62 carefully sequenced activities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sequences of activities that scaffold from accessible explorations to more challenging problems; ensure activities build toward targeted habits (proof, modeling, communication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-test and adapt materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials were field-tested at thirteen universities and colleges; courses should be adaptable to different institutional contexts and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot materials with real student populations, collect feedback, and adapt content scope, pacing, and difficulty to institutional constraints and student preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include core discrete topics (graph coloring, isomorphism, trees, bipartite, planar, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Course topics include "graph coloring, properties of graphs, isomorphic graphs, regular and irregular graphs, trees, bipartite graphs, planar graphs, and applications of graphs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure semester curricula devote substantial time to these graph-theory topics and provide classroom lessons that can be transferred to K–8 settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Springboard to other mathematical conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities should springboard into other conversations such as even/odd numbers, counting problems, methods of proof, constructing examples and counterexamples, and problems like the Four Color Theorem and the Traveling Salesman Problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discrete tasks to introduce proof techniques, parity arguments, enumeration, counterexamples, and open problems to motivate deeper mathematical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach systematic listing and organization (tree diagrams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tree diagrams and systematic recording to organize choices and ensure completeness when listing possibilities (e.g., perfect matchings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and require systematic combinatorial strategies rather than random trial; use tree diagrams so students can prove they have found all possibilities and avoid duplicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize reasoning, justification, and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Build an environment of sense-making that "ultimately leads to formal proof" and develops mathematical communication skills so students can convince peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students present solutions, justify conclusions publicly, critique peers' arguments, and practice constructing complete proofs arising from activity work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use games and game trees for structured case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use games (e.g., Conway’s Game of Sprouts) to have students generate all possible responses and build game trees to determine winners and create proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate collaborative generation of move-lists (color-coded Post-Its example), build a game tree with the class, and use it to teach exhaustive case analysis and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ human-graph and kinesthetic activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Human graphs: students act as vertices and yarn as edges to demonstrate graph properties, parity of degrees, coloring, outerplanarity, and cooperation/communication skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tactile activities for kinesthetic learners; design tasks (e.g., coloring by holding colored sheets) that surface graph-theoretic principles and foster collaboration and nonverbal problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, collaborative classroom structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes feature short interactive lectures followed by group work (3–4 students), representatives presenting solutions on the board, and whole-class discussions emphasizing justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a comfortable atmosphere where students are challenged by peers, construct content knowledge together, and learn to critique and interpret multiple approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment aligned to practice and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment examples include weekly homework, quizzes, two midterms and a final, and project-based assessments such as redesigning lesson plans and teaching a lesson with written reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine traditional assessments (quizzes/exams) with authentic tasks (lesson redesign, teaching practice, reflective writing) to measure content mastery and ability to translate to classroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align curriculum with standards and certification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses should prepare graduates to "introduce [discrete mathematics topics] to their students" and be mindful of state/NCTM/Common Core contexts (though CCSS may not explicitly list discrete topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map course outcomes to NCTM recommendations and relevant state licensure/endorsement requirements; adapt emphasis where standards or exams (e.g., Praxis II) require particular content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make mathematics engaging and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrete mathematics' strength lies in being contemporary, accessible mathematics where students learn behaviors of mathematical practice; it attracts, excites, and engages students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-world connections, games, maps, and problems perceived as relevant to motivate student interest and develop problem-solving persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize depth over breadth (flexible coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In capstone and activity-based courses "there is no pressure to cover a set amount of material" and freedom to spend necessary time on fruitful challenging problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow pacing flexibility to follow rich problems deeply rather than forcing completion of a fixed topic list; focus on habits of mind and deep understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manipulatives, models, and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Course includes methods of teaching the content using physical materials, models, technology, and middle school curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate hands-on materials (paper plates, masking tape, yarn), visual models (floor plans), and available technology to support exploration and classroom transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate and adapt complexity for the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Some text or topics may be skipped because "it was too difficult for the audience"; courses are offered to varied audiences (undergraduates, practicing teachers, graduate students) and should be adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust depth and selection of activities for the preparation level and goals of the students (e.g., practicing teachers vs. undergraduates), and provide supports or alternate resources as needed.
